planting.note: Plant dormant container plants in winter to early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil; Southland ripens mid-to-late season over an extended picking window and needs a second rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Brightwell nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur well before planting; Southland is an older University of Georgia rabbiteye release grown across zones 7B-9A, valued for producing large numbers of sweet, large berries over a long mid-to-late season harvest window rather than one heavy flush. Plants are vigorous and reliably productive in the humid Gulf South once established, but fruit set and berry size improve substantially with a second, overlapping-bloom rabbiteye cultivar planted within about 50 feet, since Southland is not self-fruitful. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summer heat, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Windy is a low-chill, early-flowering, early-ripening rabbiteye from a Florida 79-19 x Florida 79-27 cross and needs a second early-blooming rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Windy was bred from a Florida 79-19 x Florida 79-27 cross specifically for its unusually low chilling requirement among rabbiteyes, giving it early flowering and early ripening well suited to mild-winter zone 8-10 Gulf South gardens where higher-chill rabbiteyes bloom unevenly. The vigorous, upright plants sucker freely from rhizome buds at the base, so annual mowing or pruning of basal sprouts keeps the crown narrow and manageable. Fruit has a notably shallow calyx scar and firm texture suited to fresh eating; because Windy sets poorly alone, plant with another early rabbiteye cultivar within about 50 feet for full-sized berries. Mulch with pine bark to keep the shallow root system cool through hot, humid summers.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Small Fruit Research Station, Poplarville MS

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Springwide is a low-chill Southern highbush blueberry with an upright-to-spreading habit and should be interplanted with another Southern highbush cultivar with an overlapping bloom period for the best fruit set.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.2 with peat and pine bark fines well before planting; Springwide is a patented low-chill Southern highbush blueberry with medium plant vigor and a habit between erect and spreading, producing large, medium-blue berries with a good picking scar, firm texture, and mild flavor suited to fresh eating. Its low chilling requirement makes it a candidate for zone 8-10 Gulf South winters where Northern highbush types often underperform. Southern highbush cultivars including Springwide are self-fertile but set more and larger fruit with a second, overlapping-bloom cultivar nearby, so plant at least two varieties together. Keep the shallow, fibrous roots consistently moist with drip irrigation and a thick pine bark or pine straw mulch, and avoid phosphorus-heavy fertilizers.
sources: United States Patent and Trademark Office — Plant Patent PP16,333, Springwide Blueberry

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Magnolia needs about 500 chill hours and blooms early, so interplant with another Southern highbush cultivar with an overlapping bloom window for reliable cross-pollination and better freeze insurance.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.2 with peat and pine bark fines before planting; Magnolia was released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service breeding program at Poplarville, Mississippi, specifically for the coastal plains of the southeastern United States, and carries a moderate chilling requirement of about 500 hours. It blooms roughly 5 to 12 days after the earliest rabbiteye cultivars but its fruit often ripens 5 to 14 days ahead of them, giving growers an early harvest while reducing exposure to late-winter freeze damage during bloom. For best production, interplant Magnolia with another Southern highbush cultivar rather than growing it as a single variety block. Mulch with pine bark or pine straw to keep the shallow root system cool and moist through Gulf Coast summers, and skip lime and phosphorus-heavy fertilizers.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Small Fruit Research Station, Poplarville MS

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Santa Fe has a very low chilling requirement of about 350 hours and pairs well with other early-blooming Southern highbush cultivars such as Star or Windsor for cross-pollination.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.2 with peat and pine bark fines well before planting; Santa Fe was released by the University of Florida in 2000 with one of the lowest chilling requirements among Southern highbush cultivars, around 350 hours, making it a strong fit for zone 8-10 Gulf Coast winters that are often too mild for higher-chill blueberries. Plants are vigorous and upright, ripening medium-to-large, dark blue berries with excellent scar, firmness, and flavor from early to late May. Because it is somewhat difficult to root, buy nursery-propagated plants rather than attempting hardwood cuttings at home, and interplant with another early-blooming Southern highbush cultivar such as Star, Windsor, or Rebel for the strongest fruit set. Keep roots consistently moist with drip irrigation and a heavy pine bark mulch, since blueberries have shallow, fibrous root systems intolerant of drought.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars from the University of Florida (HS1245)

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Ira has a higher chill requirement near 700-800 hours and blooms about two days after Tifblue, so plant it alongside Tifblue or another mid-season rabbiteye for cross-pollination.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Ira is a Florida-bred rabbiteye released in 1970 with a comparatively high chilling requirement of roughly 700-800 hours, making it best suited to the cooler end of zones 7-9 rather than the deep Gulf Coast. It blooms about two days after Tifblue and has fruited reliably even in years when freeze damage reduced yields on many other rabbiteye cultivars in the Piedmont. Berries are medium-sized with average-to-good firmness and scar, ripening from mid-June to late July, but their relative softness means Ira is grown more for reliability under mechanical harvest conditions than for premium fresh-market fruit. Plant with Tifblue or another overlapping-bloom rabbiteye within about 50 feet, since Ira is not self-fruitful, and mulch heavily to protect its shallow roots.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Blueberry Varieties for Florida (HS967)
